title: Sets and classification
part: Part IV · Shape, structure and measure
soi: Sets organise membership and overlap; clear definitions and representations prevent double counting and make survey claims testable.
engage: When two groups overlap, what can we know about the missing intersection, and how does that change a decision?
atl: In order for a student to organise information, students must define categories, represent overlap, check totals and explain how a definition changes a conclusion.
objectives: Use set notation, elements and subsets.
Represent union, intersection and complement with Venn diagrams.
Classify number families and place values on the real line.
Interpret survey counts and justify decisions with stated denominators.
vocabulary: set · element · subset · empty set · universal set · union · intersection · complement · Venn diagram · natural · whole · integer · rational · irrational · real

sections.title: Sets, elements and subsets
sections.intent: Define a set clearly, list each element once and distinguish “element of” from “subset of”.
paras: A set is a well-defined collection. x [[math:\in]] A means x is an element of A; B [[math:\subseteq]] A means every element of B is also in A. Order and repeated listings do not change a set.
The empty set [[math:\emptyset]] has no elements and is a subset of every set. A set with n distinct elements has 2ⁿ subsets, because each element is either included or excluded.

example.title: Subsets of {a,b,c}
example.problem: Choose included or excluded for each element.

sections.warning: [[math:\in]] relates an element to a set; [[math:\subseteq]] relates one set to another. {a} [[math:\subseteq]] {a,b}, but a [[math:\in]] {a,b}.

practice.prompt: List the elements of A = {even numbers from 1 to 10}.
practice.reasoning: Apply the membership rule once to each candidate.

verify.expr: [n for n in range(1,11) if n%2==0]

practice.prompt: How many subsets has a 3-element set? A 4-element set?
practice.reasoning: Use 2ⁿ.

practice.prompt: Are {1,2,2,3} and {3,2,1} the same set? Explain.
practice.answer: Yes. Repetition and order do not matter; both contain exactly 1, 2 and 3.
practice.reasoning: A set records membership, not listing order.

practice.prompt: For A={a,b}, decide: a[[math:\in]]A, {a}[[math:\subseteq]]A, [[math:\emptyset]][[math:\subseteq]]A, {a}[[math:\in]]A.
practice.answer: True, true, true, false (unless {a} itself were listed as an element).
practice.reasoning: Distinguish elements from subsets.

practice.prompt: A club chooses any subset of 5 activities, including none. How many choices?
How many subsets of {1,2,3,4,5} contain 1?
practice.reasoning: Fix 1 as included; choose freely among the other four.

diagram.caption: Each element has two choices: in or out. Three elements give 2³ = 8 subsets.

sections.title: Venn diagrams and set operations
sections.intent: Place the overlap first, then the “only” regions, then the outside region.
paras: Union A [[math:\cup]] B contains elements in A or B or both. Intersection A [[math:\cap]] B contains elements in both. Complement A′ contains elements in the universal set [[math:\xi]] that are not in A.
For finite sets, n(A[[math:\cup]]B)=n(A)+n(B)−n(A[[math:\cap]]B). Subtract the overlap once because it was counted in both totals.

example.title: Complete a Venn diagram
example.problem: [[math:\xi]] has 30 students; 17 help at a fair, 14 at a concert, 6 at both.

sections.warning: “A or B” in mathematics includes both unless the question says “exactly one”.

practice.prompt: A={1,2,3,4}, B={3,4,5}. Find A[[math:\cup]]B and A[[math:\cap]]B.
practice.reasoning: Union collects all; intersection keeps shared elements.

practice.prompt: In a 30-student group, 17 like F, 14 like C and 6 like both. Find all four Venn regions.
practice.answer: F only 11; both 6; C only 8; neither 5.
practice.reasoning: Subtract the overlap from each total; subtract the union from 30.

practice.prompt: Why is n(A[[math:\cup]]B) not always n(A)+n(B)?
practice.answer: The intersection is counted twice, so subtract it once.
practice.reasoning: Use inclusion–exclusion.

practice.prompt: Of 40 people, 22 take tea, 18 take coffee and 7 take both. How many take neither?
If A[[math:\subseteq]]B, what are A[[math:\cap]]B and A[[math:\cup]]B?
practice.reasoning: Every element of A is already in B.

practice.prompt: n(A)=12, n(B)=9 and n(A[[math:\cup]]B)=17. Find n(A[[math:\cap]]B).

sections.title: Number sets and the real line
sections.intent: Classify a number by the sets it belongs to, not by the way it is written.
paras: Natural numbers [[math:\mathbb{N}]] are counting numbers (here 1,2,3,…); whole numbers add 0; integers [[math:\mathbb{Z}]] add negatives; rationals [[math:\mathbb{Q}]] are ratios of integers with nonzero denominator. Real numbers [[math:\mathbb{R}]] include rationals and irrationals.

Thus natural numbers are a subset of whole numbers, which are a subset of integers, which are a subset of rationals, which are a subset of reals. A terminating or repeating decimal is rational. Non-repeating, non-terminating decimals such as √2 and π are irrational.

example.title: Classify −3, 0, 0.75 and √2
example.problem: Use the most specific familiar set, then note wider membership.
example.answer: All four are real; only √2 is irrational.

sections.warning: A number can belong to several sets. “Rational” does not mean “fraction-looking”; 0.5 and 1/2 are both rational.

practice.prompt: Classify −4, 0, 5 and 1/2 as natural, whole, integer, rational or real (give the most specific listed).
practice.answer: −4 integer; 0 whole; 5 natural; 1/2 rational. All are real.
practice.reasoning: Use the nesting of number sets.

practice.prompt: Which are irrational: √2, π, 0.25, 1/3?
practice.reasoning: 0.25=1/4 and 1/3 are ratios of integers.

practice.prompt: Is every integer rational? Is every rational an integer?
practice.answer: Yes; no. For example −3=−3/1 is rational, but 1/2 is not an integer.
practice.reasoning: Integers are a subset of rationals.

practice.prompt: Place −2, 0, 1/2 and 2 on a number line in order.
practice.reasoning: Negative values lie left of zero.

practice.prompt: Explain why 0.333… is rational.
practice.answer: It equals 1/3, a ratio of integers.
practice.reasoning: Repeating decimals are rational.

practice.prompt: Find a rational and an irrational number between 1 and 2.
practice.reasoning: 1.5 lies between; √2≈1.414 also lies between.

diagram.caption: Natural numbers sit inside whole numbers, integers, rationals and reals. Irrationals are real but not rational.

sections.title: Sets in surveys and decisions
sections.intent: Define the universal set and categories before counting; state whether “or” includes overlap.
paras: A survey count is only meaningful with its universal set. “Pool users” may include people who also use the gym; “pool only” excludes them.
Use a Venn diagram or table to organise counts, check that regions sum to the total, and translate the result into a decision with a stated assumption.

example.title: A centre audit
steps: Pool only 26; gym only 19; both 18; neither 17.
At least one: 63, which is 78.75% of 80.

sections.warning: A percentage needs its denominator. 37/80 and 19/80 answer different questions about gym use.

practice.prompt: 80 members: 44 pool, 37 gym, 18 both. Find the four regions.
practice.reasoning: Subtract overlap, then subtract union from 80.

practice.prompt: What percentage use at least one facility?
Is “more than a third use the gym” true? Discuss both meanings.
practice.answer: Yes for all gym users: 37/80=46.25%. No for gym only: 19/80=23.75%.
practice.reasoning: The category definition changes the claim.

practice.prompt: Pool-only pass $4, gym-only $3, combined $6. Find income if each member buys the relevant pass.
practice.reasoning: Use the exactly-one and both regions.

practice.prompt: Why should a survey report state the universal set?
practice.answer: The same count can mean different proportions in different populations.
practice.reasoning: Percentages and “neither” depend on the total and the denominator.

practice.prompt: 50 people: 34 like vanilla, 29 chocolate, 7 neither. Find both and vanilla only.
practice.reasoning: Union 43; overlap 34+29−43.

explore.title: How much overlap is possible?
explore.instruction: Criterion B. Use inequalities to find the full range of a missing intersection, then justify both endpoints.
explore.intro: A committee has 30 students. 17 help at a fair (F), 14 at a concert (C). First use a stated overlap of 6; then treat the overlap x as unknown.

items.prompt: With overlap 6, find all four regions and the number helping at least one event.
items.answer: 11, 6, 8, 5; at least one 25.
items.reasoning: Subtract the overlap and use the total 30.

items.prompt: With unknown overlap x, write n(F[[math:\cup]]C) and the neither count.
items.answer: 31−x and x−1.

items.prompt: Find the smallest possible x and explain why x=0 fails.
items.answer: x=1. If x=0, the union would be 31, more than the 30 students.
items.reasoning: The union cannot exceed the universal set.

items.prompt: Find the largest possible x and describe that diagram.
items.answer: x=14. All concert helpers also help at the fair; C is a subset of F.
items.reasoning: The overlap cannot exceed either set total.

items.prompt: The committee needs 20 helpers for a combined event. With overlap 6, are there enough? Could the answer change across the possible range?
items.answer: Yes, 25 helpers. Across x=1 to 14, the union ranges from 30 down to 17, so for x≥12 there would be fewer than 20.
items.reasoning: Union = 31−x; solve 31−x≥20.

application.title: The centre audit
application.instruction: Criterion D. Simulated membership data. State the region and denominator behind every claim.
application.intro: 80 members: 44 use the pool, 37 use the gym, 18 use both. Passes: pool $4, gym $3, combined $6.

items.prompt: Complete the four regions and check the total.
items.reasoning: Pool only 44−18; gym only 37−18; neither 80−63.

items.prompt: Find pass income and the percentage using at least one facility.
Test “more than a third use the gym” under two meanings.
items.answer: All gym users: true (46.25%). Gym only: false (23.75%).
items.reasoning: State whether the overlap is included.

items.prompt: A combined pass costs $6 instead of $4+$3. Give one member argument, one centre argument and a recommendation.
items.answer: Sample: members save $1; the centre may receive less per dual user but gain simplicity and uptake. Recommend tracking visits and uptake before changing price.
items.reasoning: A fairness judgment needs a stated criterion and data.

items.reasoning: The first relates an element; the second relates sets.

items.reasoning: Subtract the overlap once.

groups.instruction: Connect ideas. Give units and reasons where requested.

items.answer: √9=3 is natural/rational; √10 is irrational.
